passages.title: Night lights and sea turtles
paragraphs: Every summer, female loggerhead turtles return to the beaches where they hatched to lay their eggs. Weeks later, the hatchlings dig their way out of the sand at night and head for the sea, guided by the brightest horizon.

On natural coasts that horizon is the ocean, which reflects moonlight. On developed coasts, however, street lamps and hotels shine more brightly than the water, and many hatchlings crawl inland instead. Researchers in Florida estimate that lighting disorients tens of thousands of hatchlings every year.

The solution is surprisingly simple. In 2015, the town of Boca Grande replaced its white lamps with amber ones, which turtles barely notice, and asked residents to close their curtains after dark. Within three seasons, disorientation reports fell by more than half.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Some business owners complained that the dimmer streets felt unsafe, and the town had to add motion sensors near restaurants. Volunteers now patrol the beach at dawn, counting tracks to check whether the hatchlings reached the water.
